item.title: I Hate React and JS
item.description:
The Vibe Coding / React Trap

There is a huge shift of Data Scientist’s moving toward AI Engineering. Given Data Science is very Python heavy, it’s hard to know which front-end framework to learn and why. So many of us will naturally turn to the vibe coding, which almost exclusively spits out huge scary folders of React code.

This was my experience, and it lead me down the road of doing a React course and spending 6 months trying to build React apps. I struggled to commit to any project for over a week until I realised that I just do not enjoy writing or editing React code at all.

HTMX as an Alternative

I came across a blog post on HTMX last week and Then I actually read the pitch: HTML attributes that let any element make an HTTP request and swap the response into the page. No JSX. No build step. No client-side state to manage, because the server just sends back HTML fragments and HTMX drops them where you tell it to.

<button hx-get="/movies/42/rate" hx-target="#rating-widget" hx-swap="innerHTML">
  Rate this movie
</button>

That’s it. That’s the whole interaction. No useState, no fetch, no useEffect, no reducer. The server does what it’s good at (logic, data, templates), and the browser does what it’s good at (rendering HTML), and HTMX is just the thin, boring glue between them.

As a Python person, the part that really sold me was realizing I didn’t need a separate API layer at all. My FastAPI endpoints could just return HTML instead of JSON, rendered straight from Jinja2 templates. Suddenly my backend skills — the thing I actually already knew — were 90% of what I needed to build a real app.

Building MovieClub

To actually test this out, I built MovieClub — a small app for my friend group to log movies we’ve watched together, rate them, and argue about rankings. Nothing groundbreaking, but exactly the kind of CRUD-y, form-heavy, “fetch data and update part of the page” app that HTMX is built for.

The stack ended up being refreshingly small:

  • FastAPI for routing and business logic (the part I already knew)

  • Jinja2 for templates

  • HTMX for interactivity — searching movies, submitting ratings, filtering by member, live-updating the leaderboard

  • SQLite because I didn’t need anything heavier for a friend group’s movie list

  • A tiny sprinkle of vanilla CSS, no framework needed A few things that used to be multi-file React ordeals became almost trivial:

  • Live search for movies: an input with hx-get="/movies/search" hx-trigger="keyup changed delay:300ms" hx-target="#results". One line of HTML. In React this was a whole controlled-input-plus-debounce-hook situation.

  • Adding a rating without a page reload: a form that posts to an endpoint and swaps in the updated rating widget. No client-side state to sync, because there is no client-side state — the server is the source of truth, always.

  • The leaderboard updating in real time as people rate movies: hx-trigger="every 5s" on a container polling an endpoint. That was genuinely a five-minute feature. Here’s the actual base template MovieClub is built on. This is, quite literally, the entire “frontend framework” for the app:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
    <title>{% block title %}movie club{% endblock %}</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="/static/css/theme.css" />
    <script src="https://unpkg.com/htmx.org@2.0.4"></script>
  </head>
  <body>
    <div class="crt"></div>
    {% if user %}
    <nav>
      <span class="logo">movie club</span>
      <span class="nav-links">
        <a href="/">month</a>
        <a href="/vote">vote</a>
        <a href="/leaderboard">leaderboard</a>
        {% if user.team_id %}<a href="/team">my team</a>{% endif %}
        <span class="dim">{{ user.name }}</span>
        <form method="post" action="/logout" class="inline">
          <button type="submit" class="linklike">logout</button>
        </form>
      </span>
    </nav>
    {% endif %}
    <main>{% block content %}{% endblock %}</main>
  </body>
</html>

What I love about this file is how boring it is. There’s nothing here I have to explain to a future version of myself. {% if user %} shows the nav if someone’s logged in. {% if user.team_id %} shows the “my team” link if they’re on one. Every other page in the app extends this template and fills in title and content. When I add a new page, I’m not thinking about component composition or where state should live — I’m just writing a Jinja2 block and maybe an HTMX attribute or two.

I deployed it on a FastAPI Cloud — no separate frontend build pipeline, no CORS configuration, no Vercel/Netlify account for the frontend and a different host for the backend. One app, one deploy.

What I Recommend it over React

Looking back at the two experiences side by side:

  • I understood every layer of my own app. With React, there was always a black box somewhere — bundler config, hook lifecycle timing, hydration quirks. With HTMX + FastAPI, I could trace a click all the way from the button, to the HTTP request, to the Python function, to the Jinja2 template, back to the DOM. Nothing felt magic.
  • My data science instincts transferred. I’m used to thinking in terms of data flowing through a pipeline. HTMX apps feel like that: request in, HTML out, swap. It’s a mental model close to how I already think about data transformations.
  • I shipped faster. MovieClub went from idea to deployed app in a weekend. My React todo-list clone from the course took me longer than that, and it did about a tenth as much.
  • Way less code, way less anxiety. No node_modules folder eating 400MB. No dependency upgrade dread. No “why did this break after a patch version bump.”
  • AI assistance became safe again. I still use AI tools to help write code for MovieClub, but now the loop is honest again. When OpenCode suggests an hx-get attribute or a FastAPI route, I can read it top to bottom and understand exactly what it does — there’s no hidden reconciliation behavior or closure trap for it to quietly get wrong. Vibe-coding a feature I don’t fully understand is much lower-risk when the “runtime” is just an HTTP request and a template render, not an entire client-side framework’s internal state machine.

Where HTMX Falls short

HTMX isn’t a universal answer, and my course wasn’t a waste. If I ever want to build something with heavy client-side interactivity — a drag-and-drop movie-ranking board, complex animations, or offline support — I know I’d probably have to reach for React or a lighter alternative like Alpine.js layered on top of HTMX for the fiddly bits. HTMX shines brightest for exactly the kind of app MovieClub is: mostly CRUD, mostly server-driven, occasionally interactive.

But for a data scientist trying to get from “I have a backend I understand” to “I have a deployed app that works,” HTMX removed almost every piece of friction that made React feel like a second full-time job. It let me build something real, ship it, and actually enjoy the process — which, three weeks into that React course, I genuinely wasn’t sure was possible.

If you’re comfortable with Python, terrified of the JavaScript ecosystem and just want to ship something — do yourself a favor and spend an afternoon with HTMX and FastAPI before you try another React course. It might save you some stress.

item.title: Movie Club: My First Deployed Full-Stack Web App
item.description:
I spend most of my time as a data scientist / AI engineer: notebooks, models, pipelines. But every model I ship eventually needs an actual application around it, and my ability to build that part has always been limited. So I built one from scratch: Movie Club, a server-rendered FastAPI app that runs a monthly film competition for my friends and me.

The dashboard — submission phase, phosphor-green CRT theme.

What is Movie Club?

Having moved from Melbourne to Berlin, I am no longer able to meet my friends for our monthly movie club competition, so I thought it is a good opportunity for my first deployed application to make an app for us. ### The Rules: Every month each team member submits one movie. Everyone watches and ranks all the picks best → worst. The top film wins; the bottom film sends its submitter to the bench (they still vote next month, but can’t submit). Repeat forever.

Live: https://movieclub.fastapicloud.dev

The product

The whole thing runs on a three-phase cycle lifecycle:

  1. SUBMITTING — each member picks one film via live search against the OMDB API. One pick per person, no duplicates.
  2. RANKING — an admin locks submissions, then everyone drags their ballot into order with ▲▼ controls.
  3. CLOSED — points are tallied by Borda count: position 1 of N films gets N−1 points, last place gets 0. Winner crowned, loser evicted, next cycle auto-created.

Joining is invite-only via a team code, and an all-time leaderboard tracks wins and losses per member.

The /vote ballot page, built as HTMX partials so reordering never reloads the page.

The all-time leaderboard. Bragging rights are permanent.

The stack

I deliberately avoided React. The goal was to learn how a “real” web app works at the request/response level, not to learn a frontend framework:

Layer Choice
Hosting FastAPI Cloud
Backend FastAPI + Jinja2 templates + HTMX fragments
Database PostgreSQL via SQLAlchemy 2.0, Alembic migrations (Supabase in prod)
Auth Argon2 password hashing + signed session cookie (itsdangerous)
Movies OMDB API
Styling Hand-rolled CSS, black/phosphor-green CRT theme

The architecture is refreshingly boring:

browser → router → SQLAlchemy model → template or redirect

Routes return either full pages or HTML fragments. HTMX swaps fragments into placeholders (#ballot, #search-results) — no SPA, no client state, no build step. For a voting app where interactions are small and local, this felt exactly right.

Next: Building a Recommender System

Here’s the part I’m most excited about. This little club is quietly generating a dataset:

  • Every member’s full ranking of shared movies, every month, indefinitely
  • Implicit signals: abstentions, submission choices, win/loss history
  • A growing matrix of members × movies with ordinal preferences

The obvious problem with a 6-person club is sparsity — six months in, we might have 30 movies total. The fix: Letterboxd exports. Letterboxd lets any user export their entire diary and ratings as CSV (title, year, rating, watched date). Importing those gives every member hundreds of rated films immediately.

The plan:

  1. Members upload their Letterboxd export (or connect via the unofficial API).
  2. Normalize ratings onto a common scale and align with OMDB/IMDb IDs.
  3. Train an implicit-feedback model (probably start with simple matrix factorization, then something like implicit ALS or a neural CF model) on the union of club rankings + Letterboxd ratings.

Suddenly the cold-start problem mostly disappears: a new member arrives with years of taste already attached.

item.title: Deutsch Class: Fully Local German Vocabulary Trainer
item.description:
Is there any need for yet another Language learning platform?

Having recently moved to Berlin, I wanted to practice and expand my German vocabulary, I was struggling prioritizing between my German practise and ML projects. So I built Deutsch Class: a fully local German learning app with a Postgres-backed vocabulary database, a FastAPI REST API, and a terminal UI. Everything runs on my machine.

Architecture

The whole thing is three small pieces:

┌───────────┐   HTTP    ┌──────────────┐   SQL    ┌────────────────┐
│  TUI      │ ────────► │  FastAPI     │ ───────► │  PostgreSQL    │
│ (Textual) │           │  api/main.py │          │  deutsch_class │
└───────────┘           └──────────────┘          └────────────────┘
  • PostgreSQL stores ~1,000 words seeded from a JSON file (402 easy · 402 medium · 196 difficult), each with a phonetic transcription, English translation, and a learned flag.
  • FastAPI exposes listing, search, filtering, CRUD, random draws, and stats.
  • Textual drives the terminal frontend against the live API.

The schema is deliberately simple, with difficulty constrained at the database level:

CREATE TABLE words (
    id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    word        TEXT NOT NULL,
    phonetic    TEXT,
    translation TEXT,
    difficulty  TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (difficulty IN ('easy', 'medium', 'difficult')),
    learned     BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
    UNIQUE (word, difficulty)
);

One entry point (main.py) starts the API and launches the TUI together, so uv run main.py is all you need.

The TUI

Textual made the terminal frontend genuinely pleasant to build. The main screen has a filterable word table, a search box, and a detail panel for the selected word.

Keybindings are kept minimal:

Key Action
r Draw a random word
l Toggle learned on selected word
p Pronounce the selected word (TTS)
t Test pronunciation of the selected word (mic+ASR)
/ Focus the search box
F5 Refresh the word list
q Quit

Random draw mode is where most of the studying happens — pull a random unlearned word at your chosen difficulty, hear it spoken, mark it learned when you’ve got it.

Text-to-speech

Every word shown is announced aloud using macOS say with a German voice. Pressing p replays the currently selected word. It’s a tiny feature but it completely changes how the app feels — you’re not just reading, you’re hearing the language constantly.

Pronunciation testing with on-device Whisper

This is the part I’m most happy with. Press t and the app records 3 seconds from your microphone, transcribes the audio locally with mlx-whisper using whisper-large-v3-turbo-german-f16 (a German-optimized model that runs fast on Apple Silicon), then scores your attempt against the target word via character-level edit distance:

  • ≥ 80% — green
  • 50–79% — yellow
  • < 50% — red

No audio ever leaves the machine. The first run downloads the ~1.6 GB model; after that it’s instant.

The API

The API is thin but complete — interactive docs come free with FastAPI at /docs.

Method Endpoint Description
GET /words List/filter/search words
GET /words/random Random word (filter by difficulty, unlearned only)
POST /words Create a word
PATCH /words/{id} Update any subset of fields
POST /words/{id}/toggle-learned Flip the learned flag
DELETE /words/{id} Delete a word
GET /stats Counts per difficulty + learned + total 
curl "localhost:8000/words/random?difficulty=easy&unlearned_only=true"
# {"word":"geradeaus","phonetic":"ɡərˈɑdeːˌaʊs","translation":"straight ahead",
#  "difficulty":"easy","id":294,"learned":false}

What’s next

The code is on GitHub. If you have an Apple Silicon Mac and a Postgres instance lying around, uv sync && uv run main.py gets you using it right away.

item.title: Berlin - Blog Refresh
item.dc:creator: Lucas Hudson
item.description:
Berlin - Blog Refresh

My partner and I have made the difficult decision to leave our lives, jobs and cat in Melbourne, and journey over to Berlin for a new life and new experiences. The past 10 years in Melbourne (and Canberra) have been transformative, from High School graduates through to Masters-educated practising professionals in our respective fields (Data Science and Architecture) we cannot thank our home country enough for the opportunities and experiences.

However, we had always wondered what opportunities and lifechanging experiences might come from moving overseas and we always had a vague plan to seek them. Last year, we decided it was time to organise and make some definitive plans to move, Lucy exhausted herself building matrices that cross checked lifestyle and culturual factors with opportunities and cost of living etc. This allowed us to easily decide on Berlin as the city which suited us the best, and since then had built plans to move.

Now, having moved in just a week ago, it feels like we have made an excellent decision. Walking around the streets of Kreuzberg I am overcome with feelings of inspiration, excitement and spontanaeity. I am determined to build myself into this city through engaging with the many events, cultural experiences, meetups and work opportunities, as well as let the city educate and shape a new way of life for me and guide my approach in life decisions.

This brings me to resetting my blog, I decided the cheap efforted projects I have done in the past do not align with the new approach I want to use when building personal projects. I was to make use of my skills to build projects that:

  • I find fun!
  • Only use open source models
  • Do not require big cloud providers
  • I am able to use regularly to motivate myself to improve them.

Aside from this, I want to be studying new areas of computer science and using this blog to collate my notes. So from this day onwards, expect posts much more frequently with fun projects I find enjoyable as well as my learnings.

First up, my next project being built is a local application users can practise German with, democratizing Voice and STT models to English speaking users learning German.

Hopefully will post with an update again this week!

Lucas.
